query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially homogeneous, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, exposure to intermediate temperatures (e.g., 700°C) combined with mechanical loading at service-relevant strain rates triggers rapid nanoclustering of principal elements (notably Ni, Cr, and Mn) at the grain boundaries. This localized clustering reduces the cohesive energy of the boundary, leading to the onset of intergranular brittle fracture under conditions where conventional alloys would instead display ductile behavior due to grain-boundary precipitation or impurity segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-homogenized, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with coarse grains (~50 μm) and uniform elemental distribution across the microstructure as verified by TEM/APT.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal aging at 700°C for predetermined durations (e.g., 0, 15, and 30 minutes) followed by tensile testing at an intermediate temperature (700°C) under defined strain rates (e.g., ~10⁻³ to 10⁻² s⁻¹). In parallel, implement in situ TEM or APT studies to monitor grain boundary compositional evolution during deformation.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant intermediate temperatures (around 700°C) and strain rates consistent with anticipated engineering applications under demanding high-temperature environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale clusters enriched in Ni, Cr, and Mn at grain boundaries, observable as localized compositional fluctuations, which lead to the formation of weak, decohesive zones.
generation.mechanism: Thermally and mechanically activated diffusion causes principal elements to segregate and form nanoclusters at the grain boundaries. These clusters deplete the surrounding matrix of strengthening solutes and create localized compositional inhomogeneities that reduce grain boundary cohesion, thereby promoting intergranular crack initiation and propagation, manifesting as brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (non-aged or lower-temperature-aged samples), the thermally aged and mechanically loaded samples will exhibit (a) measurable nanoclustering at grain boundaries via APT/TEM, (b) a transition from transgranular ductile fracture to intergranular brittle fracture in fracture surface analyses, and (c) a significant reduction in ductility (e.g., a 50% drop in elongation) while maintaining similar yield strength.
generation.baseline: Samples maintained at room temperature or thermally treated below the critical aging temperature (e.g., <500°C) under identical loading conditions, which maintain uniform grain boundary composition and exhibit ductile, transgranular fracture modes.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for service temperatures between 600°C and 700°C and strain rates on the order of 10⁻³ to 10⁻² s⁻¹; outside these boundaries (e.g., very high temperatures where rapid diffusion may homogenize compositions or very low strain rates), the kinetics of nanoclustering and its impact on grain boundary cohesion may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The critical time and temperature thresholds required for significant nanoclustering, the quantitative extent to which nanoclustering reduces grain boundary cohesion, and the potential influence of residual impurities not controlled in the sample preparation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples with identical initial microstructures. One set is aged at 700°C for 30 minutes (to induce nanoclustering), while the control set is maintained at a lower temperature where nanoclustering is negligible. Both sets undergo identical tensile tests at 700°C. Simultaneously, perform high-resolution APT and in situ TEM during deformation to assess grain boundary composition.
measurements: Quantitative APT measurements of elemental distribution at grain boundaries.
Fractography (SEM/TEM) to identify intergranular versus transgranular crack patterns.
Mechanical properties (ductility, yield strength, fracture strain) from tensile tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit significant nanocluster formation at grain boundaries (i.e., the compositional profiles are indistinguishable from the control) and do not show a statistically significant reduction in ductility or a shift to intergranular fracture mode compared to the baseline condition, then the hypothesis that thermally-induced nanoclustering governs the brittle behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation

However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries. papers.title: Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Aging experiments at 700°C combined with advanced microstructural characterization (microscopy, CALPHAD, nanoindentation) and impurity analysis
papers.findings: Trace interstitials (O, N) initially provide solid solution strengthening but later promote nanoscale phase segregation during thermal aging, causing depletion of strengthening elements near grain boundaries and overall softening.
papers.mechanism: Impurity-induced phase segregation reduces solute concentration in the matrix and creates local compositional variations (e.g., precipitate‐free zones) that can undermine grain boundary cohesion, potentially preluding brittle behavior at service temperatures.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (and a modified dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 sample)
papers.approach: Tensile and intermediate-temperature tests combined with high-resolution microstructural investigations (TEM, atom probe tomography) and chemical segregation analysis to assess grain boundary composition and fracture modes
papers.findings: In single-phase fcc HEAs, rapid nanoclustering and segregation of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) to grain boundaries at intermediate temperatures leads to intergranular cracking and ductility loss. An engineered approach using preexisting Cr-rich precipitates was shown to ‘trap’ the embrittling elements and markedly improve ductility.
papers.mechanism: Nanoclustering at grain boundaries induces localized decohesion, lowering the resistance to crack initiation despite the suppressed formation of large intermetallic phases. Redirecting segregating embrittling elements into secondary precipitates can mitigate brittle behavior.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened HEA with controlled grain boundary morphology (HT-1 with straight GBs vs. HT-2 with serrated GBs)
papers.approach: Tailored heat treatments to modify cooling rate, thereby altering grain boundary morphology, followed by tensile and creep testing at elevated temperature (650°C) and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: Samples with conventional straight grain boundaries exhibited brittle intergranular fracture and significant ductility drop at 650°C, while those with serrated grain boundaries showed a substantial improvement in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life due to more uniformly distributed strain and reduced local stress concentration.
papers.mechanism: Grain boundary serration can reduce local stress concentrations and delay the onset of intergranular cracking, providing resistance to brittle failure even at intermediate temperatures where GB segregation might otherwise promote brittleness.

established: In conventional alloys, brittleness is typically linked to grain-boundary segregation of impurities and phase precipitates.
HEAs can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation, often leading to favorable combinations of strength and ductility.
Even in nominal single-phase HEAs, local chemical heterogeneities such as nanoclustering or impurity-induced segregation can impair grain boundary cohesion.

approaches_tried.approach: Preexisting precipitation (e.g., Cr-rich σ phases) to capture segregating embrittling elements at grain boundaries
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced ductility at intermediate temperatures by mitigating rapid elemental segregation at GBs in HEAs

approaches_tried.approach: Engineered modification of grain boundary morphology (serration) via controlled cooling rates
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved resistance to intergranular brittle failure at elevated temperatures by reducing local strain concentrations

mechanisms: Nanoclustering-induced grain boundary decohesion due to segregation of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn)
Impurity-induced phase segregation leading to depletion of strengthening solutes in the matrix and local loss of cohesive strength at GBs
Grain boundary morphology (e.g., straight vs. serrated) influencing strain localization and crack initiation
disagreements: Whether the presence of precipitates in HEAs always degrades ductility (as in conventional alloys) or can be engineered to improve toughness by absorbing embrittling elements.
The relative role of intrinsic nanoclustering versus extrinsic factors (like processing-induced impurity pickup) in governing grain boundary decohesion in single-phase HEAs.
open_questions: What is the dominant mechanism governing toughness degradation in an initially single-phase HEA under service conditions?
How do service temperature and loading rate affect the kinetics of grain boundary segregation and the onset of brittle behavior in HEAs?
What are the quantitative thresholds (e.g., impurity concentration, grain boundary chemistry) that trigger the transition from ductile to brittle response in compositionally complex alloys?
opportunities: Design a controlled comparison experiment between an initially single-phase HEA and a borderline dual-phase variant where preexisting precipitates have been intentionally introduced, to monitor GB element segregation under identical thermal and mechanical loading.
Investigate the effects of varying cooling rates and impurity levels on the onset of nanoclustering at GBs through in situ high-temperature mechanical testing and advanced atomistic characterization.

Combine grain boundary morphology engineering (e.g., inducing serration) with compositional tailoring to decouple the effects of nanoclustering from overall phase stability, thereby enabling a direct test of the nanoclustering-induced brittle mechanism.

Utilize complementary computational (e.g., molecular dynamics, phase-field modeling) and experimental studies to pinpoint service and loading boundaries where the controlled hypothesis can be decisively falsified.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of thermally induced nanoclustering at grain boundaries via controlled thermal aging and mechanical loading using in situ microscopic characterization.
directions.assessment: This approach tests directly whether the emergence of nanoscale segregations of principal elements (e.g. Ni, Cr, Mn) at the formerly homogeneous grain boundaries causes intergranular decohesion and brittle behavior. The physics of diffusion‐induced clustering under intermediate temperatures is well understood in HEAs, and in situ methods (TEM, APT) can capture these nanoscale changes. It directly contrasts with conventional alloys by ruling out large precipitate formation and impurity segregation. It is feasible with state‐of‐the‐art equipment and would provide informative, time‐resolved insight into the transition from ductile to brittle behavior.

directions.direction: Compare the effect of intentionally varying ultra‐trace impurity (O, N) levels on the grain boundary structure and toughness in an otherwise identical single‐phase HEA.
directions.assessment: Controlling impurity levels could isolate whether trace elements drive weakening via phase segregation. However, modifying impurity content risks altering solid-solution strengthening and may complicate the interpretation if impurity effects overlap with nanoclustering effects. Evidence in refractory HEAs suggests impurities promote nanoscale phase separation, but the complexity of HEAs makes this test challenging yet informative.

directions.direction: Implement a pre‐existing second phase (e.g. Cr‐rich precipitates) to sequester embrittling elements and then compare with a strictly single‐phase HEA.
directions.assessment: This design tests whether engineered precipitates that absorb segregating elements can prevent nanoclustering at grain boundaries. Although analogous approaches have been applied in dual-phase HEAs (e.g., PMC6897545 records), doing a controlled comparison directly in a single-phase system tests if intrinsically the HEA loses toughness solely by nanoclustering rather than precipitate formation. However, introducing a second phase might violate the constraint of retaining a single-phase for service, unless carefully tuned.

directions.direction: Conduct advanced molecular dynamics and phase-field simulations of strain and temperature‐driven segregation in single‐phase HEAs.
directions.assessment: Simulations can predict the kinetics and spatial pattern of nanoclustering at grain boundaries and correlate these with loss of cohesion. This method supports the hypothesis by providing a theoretical critical parameter (e.g. cluster size or composition fluctuation) at which brittle behavior emerges. While theoretical, comprehensive simulation backed by experimental validation can greatly enhance understanding. Feasibility is high when combined with detailed experimental data.

directions.direction: Engineer and control grain boundary morphology (e.g., straight versus serrated) via tailored heat treatments and then correlate morphology with brittleness at service temperatures.
directions.assessment: Since grain boundary shape affects local stress concentrations and segregation tendencies, this design differentiates if the brittle behavior in HEAs stems from inherent nanoclustering (independent of morphology) or from stress localization promoted specifically by straight boundaries. Prior work (PMC9848264) shows serrated boundaries enhance ductility in HEAs, so comparing morphologies can distinguish the nanoclustering mechanism from conventional morphology-driven brittle fracture. It is a compelling but somewhat indirect test of the mechanism.

choice.direction: Investigate thermally induced nanoclustering at grain boundaries via controlled thermal aging and mechanical loading combined with in situ microscopies (e.g., TEM, APT) to directly correlate nanoscale segregation with intergranular brittle fracture.
choice.why: This direction most directly tests the hypothesis that even an initially homogeneous, single-phase HEA can develop localized nanoclustering of principal elements during service-like conditions (intermediate temperatures and high strain rates), thereby undermining grain boundary cohesion. It respects the constraint of a compositionally complex single-phase alloy and distinguishes the mechanism from conventional alloy behavior that typically attributes toughness loss to coarse precipitates or impurity segregation. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC6897545 records on nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement) supports this, and the approach is both feasible and highly informative for environment-specific performance.
